extracted.intended_audience: students, reformers, policymakers, and general readers interested in political economy and remedies for poverty
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing proposed remedies for poverty and low wages (e.g., cuts in public expenditure, education, unions, co-operation, government regulation, land redistribution) with attention to their mechanisms and ultimate effects given land monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of public expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction in the expenses of government can have no direct effect in extirpating poverty and increasing wages, so long as land is monopolized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a very large reduction in taxation (e.g., repudiating debt, disestablishing Church, disbanding army) would only add to the net produce available, but that addition would be absorbed as increased rent by landowners. Temporary improvements may occur only if reforms happen without the destruction attendant on revolution, and even then are likely to be swallowed up by increased land values (example: comparison to railroads increasing wealth but not alleviating pauperism). Note: governmental economy is desirable for democratic control and reducing corruption, but it is not a cure for poverty under land monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and economy of government as a democratic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything that tends to make government simple and inexpensive tends to put it under control of the people and to bring questions of real importance to the front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not sufficient to cure unequal distribution of wealth, evaluate proposals for whether they make government less extravagant and less independent of the people (reducing money in politics, patronage, and obscuring of fundamental issues). This is a political-democratic desideratum rather than an economic cure for poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion of education and improved habits (industry, frugality, intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education, industry, frugality, and intelligence increase the effective power of labor and can raise an individual only insofar as he is superior to the general level; they cannot raise general wages while land is monopolized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that spreading industrious habits or basic literacy will, by itself, raise wages generally. Examples/anti-patterns: when a skill or thrift becomes general, its wage premium disappears (clerk literacy formerly paid well, now ubiquitous). Improvements that increase productive power are likely to be converted into higher rent rather than higher wages. Assess whether the education genuinely 'enables a man more effectively to use his natural powers' and whether it relieves material want/leisure needed for intellectual growth. Beware of mistaking correlation (better material condition associated with better habits) for causation (habits causing improved material condition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and practical usefulness of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is only education insofar as it enables a man more effectively to use his natural powers; much schooling fails to produce practical ability or better thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational reforms by their practical outcomes (ability to work, judge, observe, and sustain oneself) rather than mere attainment of book-knowledge. Example: anecdote of college graduates unable to do anything practical; contrast with indigenous training that produces competence. Also consider that leisure and relief from want are preconditions for intellectual and moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of material security and leisure for moral/intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only as a man is relieved from the wants of his animal nature that his intellectual and moral nature can grow; compel a man to drudgery for necessities and he will lose the incentive to industry and the ability to develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating educational or moral-improvement proposals, account for whether they address material misery—without relieving want and providing leisure, such measures will have limited effect. Temporary increases in wages might first be wasted in dissipation but will ultimately support higher industry and intelligence if material improvement is sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of workmen (trade unions) — limited aggregate effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations of workmen can advance wages in particular trades, but no general advance in wages can be secured by combination; any advance must ultimately reduce other wages or profits, or be borne by rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess union actions by their sphere of effect: they can raise wages in specific occupations but face countervailing forces—reduced relative demand for the product, entry of more workers into that trade, import competition—so gains are often temporary or localized. Practical obstacles include the difficulty of organizing all labor (a universal combination is practically impossible), destructive nature of strikes (they lessen wealth), and the necessary internal tyranny of organizations preparing for strikes. Weigh the destructive costs of strikes and organization against the limited benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the true opposing interest: landowners, not capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The real contest over wages is between laborers on the one side and the owners of land on the other; landowners can endure deadlocks that labor cannot because land does not 'go to waste' like capital and its owners can 'wait.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating industrial conflict strategies, recognize that increasing wages generally would require reducing rent; in broad deadlocks the laborers are more vulnerable (starvation/emigration) while landowners can wait out the struggle. Examples: agricultural laborers versus farmers versus landowners; historical ease with which landowners 'combine' due to fixed nature of land and certain tendency of land value to rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-operation (in supply and production) — limited systemic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-operation in supply reduces the cost of exchanges; co-operation in production increases the efficiency of labor—but both, when generalized, tend to increase rent rather than raise general wages under land monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish isolated/co-operative successes from generalizable remedies. Co-op in supply saves labor and risk (like improved exchanges) and therefore tends to add to rent; co-op in production substitutes proportionate wages (a 'lay') and increases efficiency, again producing increased rent. Co-operation between producers and landowners is effectively rent-in-kind. Evaluate co-operation by whether it addresses land monopoly or only reduces transaction costs or increases efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental direction/interference and socialism
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution of governmental direction for individual action (socialistic regulation) substitutes restriction for freedom, involves large bureaucratic/inquisitorial powers, risks demoralization and corruption, reduces incentives to accumulation, and is impractical in modern society if attempted by fiat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess state-centered remedies by administrative burden, incentive effects, and feasibility of large-scale implementation. Specific concerns: graduated income tax requires many officials with inquisitorial powers and invites evasion, bribery, perjury; elaborate schemes for regulating employment risk creating demoralizing bureaucracy (historical comparisons: ancient Peru, Jesuit Paraguay). The author concedes the ideal of socialism is noble and perhaps possible, but insists it must 'grow' organically rather than be engineered by modern governments lacking requisite unifying faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: More general distribution of land (land-tenure reforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A more general division of landed property (free trade in land, tenant right, equal partition among heirs, restrictions on holding size, state buy-outs, or grants for colony settlement) is commonly proposed as connected to social distress, but each proposal must be assessed for its ability to actually break land monopoly and avoid unintended abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate land-tenure proposals on whether they would actually diminish the monopolization of land and so prevent increases of rent from absorbing gains. The text is skeptical about simple measures: 'free trade in land' may merely allow ownership to take the form to which it tends; state buy-outs raise complex issues; grants of public money or credit for settlements risk abuses and demoralization. Consider likely practical consequences, modes of implementation, and whether a proposal addresses the root (monopoly of land) rather than cosmetic or transactional barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central test for any proposed remedy: effect on land monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Any remedy that increases productive power, reduces costs, or spreads skills will not raise general wages if land remains monopolized—such gains become increased rent; therefore the decisive criterion is whether the remedy destroys or neutralizes the monopoly of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this overarching metric to judge the effectiveness of measures (public-economy cuts, education, unions, co-operation, government intervention, land distribution): if the policy leaves land monopoly intact, expect benefits to be captured as rent and little lasting improvement for the lowest-paid laborers. Prefer measures that directly change land tenure or the distribution of land/rent to those that only increase productive capacity or reduce costs.
